title: Teaching machines to guess
tagline: Eighty years of trying to get a program to improve at something nobody told it how to do — including two long stretches when everyone agreed it would not work.

events.title: A Logical Calculus of Nervous Activity
events.summary: Models a neuron as a threshold gate, and shows that a network of them can compute any logical proposition.
keyPoints: The neuron is reduced to weighted inputs and a firing threshold.
Networks of these units are shown to be computationally universal.
There is no learning rule yet — the weights are set, not found.
Von Neumann cited it while designing stored-program machines.
events.impact: Established the unit that every neural network since has been built from, and the idea that cognition might be a computation rather than a mystery.

resources.label: A Logical Calculus of the Ideas Immanent in Nervous Activity

events.title: Computing Machinery and Intelligence
events.summary: Replaces "can machines think" — which he calls too meaningless to discuss — with a question that can actually be settled by observation.
keyPoints: The imitation game is a proposal about evidence, not a definition of mind.
Nine objections are stated and answered, including the ones still raised today.
Suggests building a child machine and educating it, rather than programming an adult one.
Predicts learning machines, and misses the timeline by about half a century.
events.impact: Framed the entire field's evaluation problem. Every benchmark since is an attempt to make "is it working" answerable without appealing to what the system understands.

events.title: The perceptron
events.summary: The first network that finds its own weights — and the first time a machine-learning result got ahead of itself in the press.
keyPoints: A learning rule: adjust weights in proportion to the error on each example.
The convergence theorem guarantees it finds a separator if one exists.
Built as physical hardware — the Mark I Perceptron, with motor-driven weights.
The guarantee is only about linearly separable problems, which is the whole story.
events.impact: Introduced learning from examples as an engineering method. It also set the field's recurring pattern: a real result, oversold, followed by a correction that overshoots.

events.title: Perceptrons
events.summary: Proves precisely what a single-layer network cannot do, and is read by a generation as proving that neural networks cannot do anything.
keyPoints: XOR is not linearly separable, so one layer cannot learn it.
The book is careful about the single-layer case and speculative about deeper ones.
No practical way to train multiple layers existed yet, which made the point moot.
Funding moved to symbolic AI, and neural work went quiet for over a decade.
events.impact: The first AI winter's proximate cause. It is also a lesson in how a correct, narrow result travels: the proof was about one architecture, the reception was about a whole approach.

events.title: Back-propagating errors
events.summary: Gives the multi-layer network the training method it had been missing for seventeen years: send the error backwards and let the chain rule do the accounting.
keyPoints: Gradients of the loss with respect to every weight, computed layer by layer.
Hidden layers can now learn useful intermediate representations.
The technique had been derived several times before; this is when the field noticed.
It works — and in 1986 there is neither the data nor the compute to show how well.
events.impact: Still the algorithm. Every deep network trained today is doing this, and the 26-year gap before it paid off is the field's best evidence that a method can be right and premature at the same time.

events.title: LSTM
events.summary: Gates that let gradients survive long sequences, solving the vanishing-gradient problem.

events.title: Support vector machines
events.summary: Margins and kernels win the 1990s on small data, and neural nets wait their turn.

events.title: Dropout
events.summary: Randomly deleting units during training stops a big network memorising its data.

events.title: Adam
events.summary: An optimiser with sensible defaults, which quietly removed a whole class of tuning.

events.title: LeNet-5
events.summary: A convolutional network reading handwritten digits on real cheques — deep learning's first quiet commercial success.
keyPoints: Convolution shares weights across positions, so a feature is learned once, not per pixel.
Pooling gives tolerance to small shifts without being told about them.
The architecture encodes a prior about images rather than learning it from scratch.
Deployed at scale in banking while the wider field remained sceptical.
events.impact: Showed that architectural priors beat brute force when data is limited, and produced the template — convolution, pooling, repeat — that AlexNet would scale up fourteen years later.

resources.label: Gradient-Based Learning Applied to Document Recognition

events.title: ImageNet
events.byline: Deng, Dong, Socher, Li, Li & Fei-Fei
events.summary: Fourteen million labelled images, assembled on the argument that the bottleneck was not the algorithms but the data they were being starved of.
keyPoints: Built with crowdsourced labelling, which made the scale affordable.
Organised by WordNet, so the categories have structure rather than being a flat list.
The annual challenge gave the field a shared, public scoreboard.
A dataset published as a research contribution in its own right.
events.impact: Turned progress into something measurable and comparable, which is what let the 2012 result be unambiguous. Most of the field's step changes since have arrived as a dataset plus a scoreboard.

resources.label: ImageNet: A Large-Scale Hierarchical Image Database

events.title: AlexNet
events.summary: Wins ImageNet by ten points over the next entry, using ideas from 1986 and two consumer graphics cards.
keyPoints: Trained on two GTX 580s for about a week — the compute was the unlock.
ReLU activations and dropout made a network that deep trainable at all.
The margin was large enough that the result could not be argued with.
Nothing in it required a theoretical breakthrough; it required scale.
events.impact: Ended the second AI winter in a single afternoon of results, and redirected the industry's capital toward GPUs, data collection, and depth.

resources.label: ImageNet Classification with Deep Convolutional Neural Networks

events.title: GANs
events.summary: Two networks trained against each other, and generative modelling becomes a live field.

events.title: ResNet
events.summary: Skip connections let gradients reach the bottom of a very deep stack.

events.title: AlphaGo
events.summary: Search guided by learned value and policy networks beats a top human at Go.

events.title: Diffusion models
events.summary: Learn to reverse noise, and image generation stops being adversarial.

events.title: The Transformer
events.summary: Drops recurrence, so a sequence model can finally use every accelerator you point at it.
keyPoints: Self-attention makes every position one step from every other.
Training parallelises across the sequence, not just across the batch.
Cost is quadratic in sequence length — the line item that defines the follow-on research.
Presented as a translation result; it was an architecture result.
events.impact: Made model quality a function of compute spent. Once scaling laws made that explicit, capability became a budgeting exercise and the field's constraint moved to data centres.

events.title: AlphaFold 2
events.summary: Predicts protein structure accurately enough to be used instead of an experiment — a result judged by biologists, not by a leaderboard.
keyPoints: Attention over evolutionary sequence alignments plus explicit geometric structure.
Accuracy at CASP14 was competitive with experimental determination.
Predicted structures for over 200 million proteins were released openly.
Domain structure is built into the architecture — it is not a generic model pointed at biology.
events.impact: The clearest case of machine learning producing a scientific result rather than a benchmark score, and the strongest argument that encoding domain structure still beats scale alone.

resources.label: Highly accurate protein structure prediction with AlphaFold
